title: They asked for space and I'm spiralling
blurb: For the stretch between someone stepping back and you finding out what it meant.
entry_signals: I don't know if they're coming back
how long is this going to last

steps.ask: Where are you, one to ten?

steps.title: First, the next hour
steps.say:
This is the state the whole pattern is organised around: the thing you'd normally reach for to feel better is the one person currently unavailable.

That's a genuinely hard position and it isn't a character flaw. But nothing you send from here will read the way you intend it to.

One thing that helps more than it sounds like it should: put the need somewhere other than this relationship for the next hour. Not instead of them — alongside. The muscle that's underdeveloped is the one that doesn't route everything through a single person.
cites: I Can Only Feel Better Through Someone Else

steps.ask: When they asked for space — was anything in how they did it something you'd flag if a friend described it?
steps.help: Space asked for kindly and space used as punishment are different things, and only one of them is yours to sit with.

options.label: Yes — the way it happened wasn't okay
No — they were decent about it

steps.title: That part is real
steps.say:
Then the thing to look at is what they did, not how you're taking it.

Space used to punish, to control, or to avoid ever having a conversation is a pattern in its own right, and reading your reaction to it as oversensitivity is how it gets to keep working.

Write down what happened plainly, and tell someone who knows you both less than you do.

steps.help_a: As close to their words as you can get. Not your summary of it.
steps.help_b: The version that's been running since. "I need a few days" and "this is over and they're being kind about it" are different sentences.

steps.ask: What do you think space means to them?
steps.help: Worth asking because it usually means something quite different at each end. For one person it can be how they stay in a relationship; for the other it can look like the beginning of leaving.

options.label: It's how they regulate — they come back
I think it's how it ends
I genuinely don't know — we've never talked about it

steps.ask: What have you been doing with the time?
steps.help: Honestly. Drafting messages you don't send, checking whether they're online, re-reading things, telling the story to friends on a loop — all of it counts and none of it is shameful.

steps.ask: What would you need agreed, for space to be survivable rather than unbearable?
steps.help: Usually this turns out to be smaller than expected — how long, and who reaches out first. Notice that this is something they'd have to agree to, which means it has to be asked for rather than assumed.

steps.ask: And what's the version that doesn't require them at all?
steps.help: The thing you'd do regardless of what they decide. Not a threat, not a strategy to make them respond — just the part of this that stays in your hands.

steps.say: Two lists: what needs agreeing, and what doesn't. The second one is the one you can start on tonight.
